A_target.statement:
There is no [[Definition:Total Recursive Function|total computable function]] $H$ such that for all programs $p$ and inputs $x$:
:$\map H {p, x} = 1 \iff p$ [[Definition:Halting|halts]] on input $x$
That is, the [[Definition:Halting Problem|halting problem]] is [[Definition:Undecidable|undecidable]].

B_source.statement:
Let $\sequence {r_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of mappings $r_i: I \to X$, with $X$ having at least two elements.
Then there exists $d: I \to X$ such that:
:$\forall i \in I: \map d i \ne \map {r_i} i$

substitutions.row i: behavior of program i on input i
substitutions.diagonal entry: whether program i halts on i
substitutions.the anti-diagonal object: a program D that halts iff its input does not halt on itself

derived.D differs from every program on the diag: D's self-behavior contradicts any supposed decider H

validity_conditions: Assume a total decider H(p,x). Build D(p): if H(p,p) says 'halts' then loop, else halt.
Ask whether D halts on its own code: either answer contradicts H's verdict (the diagonal flip).
The contradiction is exactly the diagonal argument transported to programs and halting.
proof_plan:
Define the program $D$ by:
:$\map D p = \begin {cases} \text {loop forever} & : \map H {p, p} = 1 \\ \text {halt} & : \map H {p, p} = 0 \end {cases}$
$D$ is computable as $H$ is.
Run $D$ on its own code $\ulcorner D \urcorner$.

If $D$ halts on $\ulcorner D \urcorner$, then $\map H {\ulcorner D \urcorner, \ulcorner D \urcorner} = 1$, so $D$ loops forever.
If $D$ does not halt, then $\map H {\ulcorner D \urcorner, \ulcorner D \urcorner} = 0$, so $D$ halts.
Both cases contradict the definition of $H$.
Hence $H$ cannot exist.
{{qed}}
